answer:
1. The animation compares buying a home with renting, using US historical data: FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates. A grid of tiles stands for 247 possible start months, beginning in January 1991. Each tile is one starting month, and it is lit if buying came out ahead over a 15-year hold. Nina is an illustrative character who owns a house, next to an apartment building.

2. Over the frames, the grid goes from a 15-year view to a "ten years" view and back to "fifteen years." In the first two frames every tile is light, and the label reads "every one (100%)". The weakest case is labeled "$79,829 ahead." In the ten-year frame, a band of tiles in the middle turns dark, so some start months did not favor buying at that shorter horizon. The last two frames switch to a scene of Nina's house and the apartment. The tag on the apartment reads "the rent tag: unchanged."

3. The animation says that in every one of the 247 historical start months, buying beat renting over 15 years. Even the worst start month left the buyer about $79.8k ahead. At 10 years the result was not universal, because some start months favored renting. The "rent tag: unchanged" label seems to say that renting leaves you with no equity and no ownership, so you pay without building anything. The "history, not a forecast" and "illustrative" labels say this is past US data and not a guarantee.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice. A viewer would probably take away that if you can hold a home for 15 years, buying has historically beaten renting. They would also see that a shorter horizon, such as 10 years, makes the result less certain.

5. The idea came from the animation itself, from the "100%," "weakest: $79,829 ahead," and "ten years" and "fifteen years" labels and the dark tiles. The advice in point 4 is my own inference. The on-screen text only says "history, not a forecast" and never tells viewers what to do.
